interview_metadata.name: Baljinder Simmons
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) ??? Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Richmond and grew up mostly around Henrico, in a house where you could smell cardamom one day and vinegar-garlic Goan fish curry the next. My dad's side was Punjabi Sikh, my mom's side Goan Catholic, so I grew up going to Diwali programs, gurdwara events with cousins, and also parish picnics and Christmas Mass with my mother's friends. My parents came to Virginia in the 1980s and worked hard, so there was always this message that you serve your family and you don't embarrass the people who sacrificed for you. In school I was the kid who liked puzzles, maps, radios, and anything with a system, but I was not always the most confident student. I went to community college after high school, started taking criminal justice and emergency management classes, but I left before finishing because I needed steady work and I was helping at home. I found my way into public safety communications in my twenties, and the first year was brutal, but it also made sense to me: listening, sorting chaos, getting help moving in the right direction. I married Lauren when I was in my early thirties, and now we have two kids, Nikhil and Maya, and we live in Glen Allen. The biggest themes in my life have been balancing pressure with care, keeping my cultures connected, and learning that if I do not manage anxiety on purpose, the job and family life can swallow me whole.

follow_ups.question: When you think of childhood, what is one ordinary scene that captures your family life?
follow_ups.response: Sunday afternoons. My mother would be cooking something coconut-based, my father would have Punjabi music or cricket on, and my sister Anita and I would be doing homework at the dining table while relatives came in and out.

follow_ups.question: What part of your education still feels unfinished to you?
follow_ups.response: The bachelor's degree. I have some college credits, and I am back part-time now because I want Emergency Management or Public Administration to be more than something I read about on my own.

follow_ups.question: Who shaped your sense of responsibility the most?
follow_ups.response: My father for discipline, my mother for patience, and later some senior dispatchers who showed me that calm is a skill, not a personality trait.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was after I had been doing call-taking for a couple of years and had my first really bad child medical call. I went home and could not sleep, and for weeks I kept hearing the mother's voice in my head. I had two choices in my mind: transfer out to a quieter county administrative job, or admit I was shaken and learn how to handle the emotional part of the work. I talked to an older dispatcher named Calvin, and he did not sugarcoat it; he told me the calls stay with you unless you build habits and talk to people who understand. I stayed, got serious about crisis intervention training, started journaling after hard shifts, and eventually became one of the people younger telecommunicators come to after difficult calls. That decision is probably why I now want to be a supervisor and build peer support rather than just climb a ladder.

follow_ups.question: What did staying in the job change about you day to day?
follow_ups.response: It made me more structured. I stopped pretending I could just shake things off and started using checklists, breathing exercises, debriefs, and exercise as part of the work, not as extras.

follow_ups.question: Do you remember when you knew you had made the right choice?
follow_ups.response: About six months later, I handled a domestic violence call and stayed steady enough to keep the caller focused until officers got there. I remember thinking, okay, I can do this without becoming numb.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it "just happened". What about you?
transcript.response: For me it was conscious. I had to choose to stay in public safety communications and also choose not to act like stress was weakness.

follow_ups.question: Was there a specific action that made it feel like a decision?
follow_ups.response: I signed up for a crisis intervention course and asked my supervisor about mentoring instead of quietly applying elsewhere.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone in your family know how close you were to leaving?
follow_ups.response: Lauren knew. I told her I was tired in a way sleep was not fixing.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. At that time, formal peer support for dispatchers was thin, and most help was informal. A better debrief process and easier counseling access would have helped.

follow_ups.question: What would useful help have looked like?
follow_ups.response: A trained peer checking in after critical incidents, not just a supervisor asking if your paperwork is done.

follow_ups.question: Did you eventually get professional support?
follow_ups.response: Yes, later I used therapy through our insurance and learned anxiety management tools that I still use.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Lauren, and she is the person who knows when I am quiet because I need rest and when I am quiet because I am carrying something from work. She works as an elementary school counselor, so our dinner conversations can get pretty heavy if we are not careful. We have two children: Nikhil, who is 12 and into robotics, soccer, and making sarcastic little comments, and Maya, who is 8 and loves drawing, dance, and helping me stir sauces. My parents live about twenty minutes away, and my mother still thinks nobody is feeding me properly unless she sends food home. My sister Anita is in Short Pump with her husband, and our kids see each other almost every other weekend. Family is not just emotional support for me; it is logistics, food, culture, and the reason I keep trying to build a steadier life.

follow_ups.question: What does a normal family evening look like when you are not working late?
follow_ups.response: Homework at the kitchen island, Lauren managing school papers, me cooking or reheating something, then we try to sit together by 6:30 before activities scatter everyone.

follow_ups.question: How do your kids connect with your cultural background?
follow_ups.response: Through food first, then holidays. They know Diwali lamps, Christmas with my mom's side, some Punjabi phrases, and they help me make butter chicken and prawn curry.

follow_ups.question: Who do you call first when something stressful happens?
follow_ups.response: Lauren first. If it is about work, I may text Calvin or another dispatcher because they understand the shorthand.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My immediate circle also includes my sister Anita, my brother-in-law Marcus, and my parents, Harjit and Teresa. We are close, though we all have busy calendars.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your parents?
follow_ups.response: Usually once a week, sometimes more if one of the kids has an event.

follow_ups.question: What is your relationship with your sister like?
follow_ups.response: Warm and teasing. She is the one who reminds me not to turn every family plan into a spreadsheet.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Outside family, my closest people are a few coworkers, especially Calvin and Denise from dispatch, because shift work creates a kind of second family. I also have friends from cricket, mostly guys from Henrico, Richmond, and the West End who are Indian, Pakistani, Caribbean, and local Virginians. On Saturday rides I am friendly with the River City Cycling Club crowd, though those friendships are more activity-based. I have one old community college friend, Omar, who I meet for coffee maybe once a month. I am not someone with a huge social circle, but the people I keep close are steady.

follow_ups.question: How often do you spend time with cricket teammates?
follow_ups.response: During season, every Sunday for matches or practice, and there is usually a group chat going all week.

follow_ups.question: Do you socialize with coworkers outside work?
follow_ups.response: A little. We grab breakfast after overnight shifts sometimes, but I try not to let work become my whole social life.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Glen Allen, in a subdivision that is mostly families, commuters, and people who like good schools and quiet streets. It is not rural, but it still has pockets of trees, walking paths, and ponds where I take photos after rain. We are close enough to Short Pump for errands and close enough to Richmond that I can get to the James River trails or work without feeling cut off. The neighborhood is pretty mixed compared with where I grew up: South Asian families, Black families, white families, some newer immigrant families. People wave, but they also respect privacy, which I appreciate.

follow_ups.question: Where do you go most often nearby?
follow_ups.response: The Kroger, the library, the kids' schools, Deep Run Park, and Indian grocery stores off Broad Street.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors know each other well?
follow_ups.response: Some do. We know the families on either side, and the kids know more neighbors than I do because they ride bikes and trade snacks.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel safe overall. Working in 911 means I am never naive about what can happen, but our street is quiet and people look out for each other.

follow_ups.question: Does your job make you notice safety differently?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. I notice address numbers, lighting, road access, and whether kids are visible near traffic.

follow_ups.question: Are there safety concerns you talk about with your children?
follow_ups.response: Mostly bike helmets, checking in before going to another house, and knowing our address if they ever need help.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is stability: schools, parks, groceries, and a calm place to come home after a loud shift. The downside is traffic near Short Pump, rising costs, and sometimes a feeling that everyone is overscheduled.

follow_ups.question: What would you change if you could?
follow_ups.response: More sidewalks connecting neighborhoods to shops and parks, and less congestion on Broad Street.

follow_ups.question: Do you see yourself staying there?
follow_ups.response: For now, yes. The kids are rooted here, and it works for our routines.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: It is me, my wife Lauren, our son Nikhil, and our daughter Maya. We have no one else living with us right now. My parents and sister visit often, but they do not stay long-term. The house is busy enough with school backpacks, work uniforms, cricket gear, and Maya's art supplies spread around.

follow_ups.question: Who is usually home during weekday mornings?
follow_ups.response: Lauren and the kids are up first, and if I worked late I am moving slower. On my afternoon shifts I help with breakfast before I leave later.

follow_ups.question: How do you divide household tasks?
follow_ups.response: Lauren handles more school communication, I handle a lot of cooking and weekend errands, and we both do laundry when it becomes impossible to ignore.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is a permanent member of the household.

follow_ups.question: No relatives staying for work or school right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed in the past year?
follow_ups.response: No, only short family visits.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: My mother may stay one night if she is helping with the kids, but that is occasional.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe every couple of months.

follow_ups.question: Anyone else overnight regularly?
follow_ups.response: No, just cousins for a holiday now and then.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everyone who usually lives here is here.

follow_ups.question: No child away at school?
follow_ups.response: No, both kids are still at home.

follow_ups.question: No long hospital stays?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My week depends on my shift, but lately I usually work Tuesday through Friday, 2 p.m. to midnight, with occasional overtime. Mornings are for school drop-off help, errands, studying, or exercise before work. Saturday is usually cycling if I am not exhausted, then family chores. Sunday during cricket season is match day, and Sunday evening is when I try to prep meals for the week. Monday is my reset day: laundry, grocery planning, maybe a hike or photography if the weather is good.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually wake up?
follow_ups.response: On workdays around 7:00, though after a late or rough shift I may need until 8:00.

follow_ups.question: When do you get quiet time?
follow_ups.response: Late morning after school drop-off or after midnight when I come home and write for ten minutes before bed.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a public safety telecommunicator for Henrico County's Public Safety Communications Center. That means I answer 911 and non-emergency calls, gather information quickly, enter calls into CAD, dispatch police, fire, or EMS units, and monitor radio traffic. My normal shift is four ten-hour shifts in the afternoon and evening, but public safety is 24/7, so holidays, overtime, and emergency staffing changes happen. I do not have a second paid job. I sometimes volunteer at safety fairs, but that is community work, not income.

follow_ups.question: What is the hardest part of a normal shift?
follow_ups.response: Switching from a routine noise complaint to a life-threatening call in seconds, then documenting everything accurately while staying calm.

follow_ups.question: Do you use Punjabi at work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, not every week, but enough that it matters. A frightened caller relaxes when they hear someone can understand them.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep a few routines because if I leave life loose, shift work takes over. I do yoga or stretching three mornings a week, meditate with an app for about ten minutes, and journal after difficult calls. I also handle a lot of the cooking, especially Sunday meal prep. For the kids, I drive to robotics or dance when my schedule allows, and I manage some of the family calendar because I like details.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually cook for meal prep?
follow_ups.response: Dal, rice, roasted vegetables, chicken curry, sometimes a Goan prawn curry if I can get good shrimp.

follow_ups.question: How consistent are you with meditation?
follow_ups.response: Pretty consistent, maybe five days a week, but sometimes only five minutes.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The main change is that I started taking an online emergency management class again, so I have carved out study blocks on Monday and Thursday mornings. Nikhil's robotics schedule also picked up, which means more driving and more calendar coordination. At work, staffing has been tight, so overtime requests have become more frequent. I have had to be stricter about sleep because if I study late after a midnight shift, I pay for it the next day.

follow_ups.question: How many hours a week do you study?
follow_ups.response: Usually six to eight hours, spread across two mornings and one weekend block.

follow_ups.question: Has overtime affected family time?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly Friday nights. Lauren and I now protect Monday dinner because it is one of the few predictable times.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: During school, the kids are up around 6:45. Nikhil gets the bus first, and Maya either rides the bus or Lauren drops her if schedules line up. After school, Nikhil has robotics one day a week and soccer in season, while Maya has dance on Wednesdays and art club when it is offered. Homework usually happens before dinner, though Nikhil will stretch it out if nobody watches him. Bedtime is around 8:30 for Maya and closer to 9:30 for Nikhil.

follow_ups.question: Who handles after-school transportation?
follow_ups.response: Lauren handles more because of my afternoon shift, but I cover Mondays and Saturdays and any morning appointments.

follow_ups.question: What do the kids do when you work late?
follow_ups.response: They text me pictures or little updates, and I leave notes in their lunchboxes if I know I will miss bedtime.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My experience is unusual because I work alongside law enforcement but I am not an officer. I talk to officers over radio every shift, and I respect how hard the work can be. At the same time, as a brown man with a beard and a Punjabi name, I have had moments where I felt watched more closely, especially in airports or traffic stops when I was younger. So I hold both truths: officers can be brave public servants, and systems can still treat people unevenly.

follow_ups.question: Have you personally had a bad police encounter?
follow_ups.response: Nothing extreme. A traffic stop in my twenties felt unnecessarily sharp, like I had to prove I belonged, but it did not escalate.

follow_ups.question: Does working dispatch change how you see officers?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I hear the fear and confusion before they arrive, so I understand the uncertainty they walk into.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: The experiences that stand out are usually work-related: officers calmly talking someone down, or a call where communication breaks down and everything becomes more dangerous. I remember those because dispatch can either lower the temperature or accidentally add confusion.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever debrief with officers after calls?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes informally, especially if radio traffic was complicated or an address was hard to locate.

follow_ups.question: What makes a good officer from your perspective?
follow_ups.response: Clear radio communication, patience, and not treating every caller like they are wasting time.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and no immediate family member has either. I have known acquaintances through work or community who had arrests, mostly alcohol-related or domestic situations, but not close family.

follow_ups.question: Has arrest ever affected someone in your wider circle?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a cricket acquaintance had a DUI years ago, and it made people talk more seriously about not driving after team gatherings.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss law enforcement with your kids?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in age-appropriate ways: be respectful, know your rights, and call for help when you need help.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential and state elections, and I have become better about local elections because local government touches my job, schools, and emergency services directly. I missed a couple of smaller elections years ago when shift work was rough, but now I usually vote early. Lauren and I will talk through school board and county issues at the kitchen table. I do not put signs in the yard often, but I take voting seriously.

follow_ups.question: What helps you remember local elections?
follow_ups.response: Calendar reminders and sample ballots. I also follow county notices because of work.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote in primaries?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially if there is a local race where the primary will decide the outcome.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as a moderate Democrat or an Independent who leans Democratic, depending on the issue. I believe in competent government because I have seen what happens when public systems are underfunded or poorly coordinated. I care about public safety, but I do not think public safety is only policing; it is mental health response, good schools, transportation, housing stability, and emergency preparedness. My family background makes me pretty committed to religious freedom and immigrant communities being treated with dignity. I am practical about budgets, and I do not think every new program is automatically good, but I do think government has responsibilities that charity cannot cover. I get frustrated with extreme language from both sides, especially when people talk about public workers like we are symbols instead of human beings.

follow_ups.question: What issues matter most to you locally?
follow_ups.response: Emergency services staffing, school quality, road safety, mental health crisis response, and keeping neighborhoods affordable enough for working families.

follow_ups.question: Are there issues where you are more conservative?
follow_ups.response: I am cautious on spending without a plan, and I value personal responsibility, but that does not mean leaving people alone when systems fail them.

follow_ups.question: How does your job shape your politics?
follow_ups.response: It makes me less ideological. On a 911 line, you hear how many problems are connected: poverty, addiction, family stress, mental illness, and sometimes violence.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more focused on mental health and crisis response over the last few years. Earlier I thought mainly in terms of police, fire, and EMS capacity, but now I think about what happens before someone reaches the crisis point. I have also become more protective of election administration and basic civic trust because misinformation makes emergency work harder too. During the pandemic and after, I saw how quickly people stopped trusting institutions. That made me value clear communication more than party slogans.

follow_ups.question: Did the pandemic change how you see government?
follow_ups.response: Yes. It showed me that communication can save lives, but confusing or politicized communication can make people tune out completely.

follow_ups.question: Have your views changed because of your children?
follow_ups.response: Yes, schools and online safety matter more to me now than they did before I had kids.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me a lot, though maybe in a quieter way than people who went to protests every weekend. I work with police, and I also know what it feels like to be read as foreign or suspicious. The Black Lives Matter movement pushed conversations that were already overdue about accountability, bias, and how often police get sent to problems that are really mental health or poverty problems. I did not agree with every slogan I heard, but I understood why people were angry. It made me listen more carefully.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk about it at work?
follow_ups.response: Carefully. Dispatch centers can be politically mixed, but some of us had honest conversations about caller assumptions and how we describe people.

follow_ups.question: Did it change how you dispatch?
follow_ups.response: It reinforced being precise and neutral, not adding assumptions to a call that officers then carry into the scene.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core issue is whether people receive equal dignity and equal protection when they need help or when they are being questioned. From dispatch, I think about language: how a caller describes a Black teenager walking, or how quickly people label someone threatening. I also think about officer safety and community trust as connected, not opposite. If communities do not trust police, calls get delayed, witnesses hold back, and everyone is less safe. Reform, to me, means accountability, training, alternatives for mental health calls, and better data.

follow_ups.question: What kind of reform seems most practical to you?
follow_ups.response: Co-responder models, stronger de-escalation training, transparent complaint processes, and dispatch protocols that flag mental health needs accurately.

follow_ups.question: Do you think your community talks about race honestly?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but often only after a national event forces it. Day to day people prefer being polite to being honest.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race in the U.S. is layered. As South Asian, I have experienced being othered, but I also know my experience is not the same as Black Americans whose families have dealt with centuries of anti-Black racism. I think immigrant families sometimes want to avoid the topic because they are focused on survival and respectability. But our kids are growing up here, and they need more honesty than just telling them to work hard and be polite. I have been thinking a lot about how to teach them pride without teaching them fear.

follow_ups.question: How do you explain race to your kids?
follow_ups.response: We talk about fairness, history, and noticing when people are treated differently. I try not to make it a lecture.

follow_ups.question: Do you see racial diversity in your daily life?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in schools, work, cricket, and the neighborhood, though diversity does not automatically mean people understand each other.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly responded through conversations, reading, and small workplace changes in how I mentor newer dispatchers. I did not join large protests, partly because of shift work and partly because I am cautious in my public role.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk with most about these issues?
follow_ups.response: Lauren, my sister, a couple of coworkers, and sometimes friends from cricket because that group has a lot of immigrant perspectives.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed any habits?
follow_ups.response: I pay more attention to descriptions on calls and challenge vague words like suspicious when they are not backed by behavior.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Lauren is probably more openly progressive than I am, especially because she sees school discipline and family stress through her work. My parents are sympathetic but sometimes uncomfortable; they grew up believing you keep your head down and do not draw attention. My sister is more direct and will call out racism faster than I will. At work, reactions are mixed. Some coworkers feel criticized by the whole conversation, while others think reform is necessary if we want public safety to mean safety for everyone.

follow_ups.question: Do these conversations cause conflict?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially with older relatives, but it usually stays respectful.

follow_ups.question: Have your children asked about it?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially after seeing news clips. We answer simply and try to keep them informed without scaring them.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say my health is decent, but I have to work at it. I have diagnosed generalized anxiety disorder, and I manage it with therapy skills, exercise, sleep routines, and mindfulness. Physically, I am a little heavier than I want to be, but cycling and cricket keep me moving. My blood pressure has been borderline at times, so my doctor keeps an eye on that. The biggest risk for me is not one dramatic illness; it is stress, poor sleep, and eating too much rich food after late shifts.

follow_ups.question: Are you on any regular medication?
follow_ups.response: I take a low-dose anxiety medication prescribed by my doctor and no blood pressure medication right now.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see a doctor?
follow_ups.response: Primary care once a year, more if something comes up, and therapy check-ins as needed.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easier because I actually like active things: cycling, hiking, cricket, and yoga. It is harder because shift work disrupts sleep and meal timing. I also love cooking with butter, coconut milk, and spices, so portion control is not my natural gift. Stress makes me crave salty snacks after midnight.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit has stuck best?
follow_ups.response: Morning stretching and Saturday rides. If it is on the calendar with other people, I show up.

follow_ups.question: What habit is hardest to change?
follow_ups.response: Late-night eating after work.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing like a major injury or surgery. The main thing was an anxiety flare last year after a stretch of difficult calls and overtime. I had chest tightness one night and got checked because in my line of work you do not ignore that. It turned out to be panic and stress, not a heart problem, but it scared me enough to restart regular therapy sessions. Since then I have been more consistent with sleep and journaling.

follow_ups.question: Did that episode affect work?
follow_ups.response: I took one sick day and then adjusted my overtime for a while.

follow_ups.question: What warning signs do you watch now?
follow_ups.response: Tight chest, racing thoughts after bed, snapping at family, and wanting to skip every healthy routine.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Anxiety has gotten in the way at times, mostly by draining my patience or sleep. I have not been unable to work long-term, but I have had days where I needed to step back from overtime to stay functional at home.

follow_ups.question: How does your family notice stress?
follow_ups.response: Lauren notices I get quiet and over-focused on small tasks. The kids notice if I am less playful.

follow_ups.question: What helps you still show up for them?
follow_ups.response: I tell Lauren directly when I am maxed out, and I keep bedtime routines simple instead of trying to be perfect.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, my mother has type 2 diabetes and some knee pain, so I help with appointments or translating medical instructions when needed, even though her English is fine. My father has high blood pressure, and he acts like checking it is optional, which drives me crazy. Lauren has had stress from school work, but no major illness. The kids are generally healthy, just the usual colds, allergies, and sports bumps.

follow_ups.question: Who coordinates your parents' care?
follow_ups.response: My sister and I share it, but I handle anything involving emergency systems or medical forms.

follow_ups.question: Does your mother's diabetes affect family meals?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I try to make more lentils, vegetables, and grilled fish when she eats with us, though she still wants rice.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We are fortunate to have insurance through my county job and Lauren's school system options, but it still takes work. Mental health appointments can be hard to schedule, especially around shifts. We have delayed dental work or therapy sessions when copays piled up, but we have not completely gone without essential care. The hardest part is time: finding an appointment, leaving work, arranging kids, and then dealing with billing.

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: I usually think of myself as an Independent who leans Democratic, or a moderate Democrat depending on the year. I am not strongly attached to party identity as a tribe. follow_ups.response: Constantly.

transcript.response: Yes, she worked for pay while I was growing up.

follow_ups.response: Mostly full time once we were both in school.

follow_ups.question: Did her schedule affect home life?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but she still somehow cooked and managed family obligations.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My mother worked as a medical office assistant. She scheduled appointments, checked patients in, handled forms, answered phones, and helped people understand basic paperwork. She was very good with older patients and immigrant families because she had patience with accents and confusion.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever visit her workplace?
follow_ups.response: Yes, sometimes after school, and I remember the smell of paper, disinfectant, and coffee.

follow_ups.question: Did her work influence you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I saw how much calm communication matters when people are worried.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked for a private medical practice in the Richmond area. They provided primary care and some specialty referrals, so the business was health care services. It was not glamorous, but it was steady and community-facing.

follow_ups.question: Was it a large office?
follow_ups.response: No, a small to medium practice where people knew each other.

follow_ups.question: Did she stay there long?
follow_ups.response: Yes, for many years.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, my dad worked for pay the whole time I was growing up.

follow_ups.question: Was he full time?
follow_ups.response: Yes, full time.

follow_ups.question: Did he work overtime?
follow_ups.response: Often.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My father worked as a maintenance technician and later a facilities supervisor. He repaired equipment, handled building systems, coordinated vendors, and responded when something broke. He was practical, careful with tools, and very serious about doing work correctly the first time.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you repair skills?
follow_ups.response: Basic ones, yes. I can troubleshoot more than I can beautifully fix.

follow_ups.question: What lesson did you take from his work?
follow_ups.response: Preparation prevents panic.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for a manufacturing and warehouse facility outside Richmond. They handled packaged goods and distribution, so keeping machinery, loading areas, electrical systems, and safety equipment running mattered. Later he supervised a small maintenance crew.

follow_ups.question: Was it physically demanding work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially when he was younger and on call for breakdowns.

follow_ups.question: Did his job feel stable?
follow_ups.response: Mostly stable, though layoffs were always a background worry.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope I have finished my bachelor's degree and moved into a supervisory role at the communications center. I want to help build a real peer-support program for dispatchers, not just a poster in the break room. I hope Lauren and I are still steady, the kids are healthy and kind, and our house feels like a place where people are fed and listened to. I want to take the family to Goa and eventually to New Zealand, but I also want simple things: better sleep, less debt, more hikes, and more patience. Professionally, I want to be the kind of supervisor who understands both the policy and the human being wearing the headset.

follow_ups.question: What is the first step toward that future?
follow_ups.response: Finish the current class, then map out the remaining credits and certifications like NIMS and CPST.

follow_ups.question: What do you want your children to remember about this stage of life?
follow_ups.response: That their parents worked hard but still showed up, cooked dinner, went to games, and made room for traditions.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, service, steadiness, and respect. Family is the center, but service gives my work meaning beyond a paycheck. I value cultural memory too: language, food, music, stories, and the idea that my kids can inherit more than one tradition without being confused. I also value calm, maybe because I know how quickly life can become chaotic. To me, being a good man is not about being loud; it is about being reliable when people need you.

follow_ups.question: What value do you practice every day?
follow_ups.response: Reliability. Show up, answer the call, pack the lunch, keep the promise.

follow_ups.question: What value do you struggle to live up to?
follow_ups.response: Patience, especially when I am tired.
